title: Alan Turing Institute wants to build a UK AI model from scratch and make it free
content:
The Alan Turing Institute wants to build a UK AI model from scratch – and release it for free to the public
Key Points
- Alan Turing Institute proposes a free, open-source British AI model built from scratch
- Government advisers want computing capacity set aside to trial it
- CST warns the UK risks becoming just a high-value AI customer
- Four recommendations include an AI Sovereignty Plan and a single accountable owner
- Health and creative data named as areas to test data access
The Alan Turing Institute wants to build a British AI model from scratch and release it free to the public. The proposal features in advice from the Council for Science and Technology (CST), which the government published on Monday (19 October).
The CST described the model as national infrastructure, an open and UK-governed asset for researchers, start-ups, small businesses, public services and the open-source community. It added that the model would not be a proprietary product for a single firm or government department.
The council recommended that the government allocate some national AI computing capacity to trial different types of models and consider the Alan Turing Institute’s proposal.
The CST is the government’s top independent advisory body on science and technology, and it advises the Prime Minister and the Cabinet.
Its co-chairs, Dame Angela McLean and Lord Browne of Madingley, sent the advice to Cabinet Office minister Kanishka Narayan in a letter dated 30 July.
Warning over UK reliance on foreign AI
“Without deliberate and urgent action, the UK risks becoming a high-value AI customer, rather than a country able to shape the technology and its usage,” the council said.
The CST said the UK should keep access to leading global AI models but should not depend on them for every use case. It added that a specialised system developed in the UK would work better in some cases.
The council defined AI sovereignty as having enough control across the AI value chain to deliver the UK’s chosen outcomes, capture economic and public value, and stay resilient under pressure.
Key recommendations
The CST made four recommendations, starting with a UK AI Sovereignty Plan built on a map of the country’s AI ecosystem.
The map would cover computing power, data, skills, models, governance and public adoption, and identify which capabilities the UK should own, share or secure access to.
The council wants these choices to shape rapid AI pilots in areas such as national security, health and education.
Each pilot would need to answer six questions:
- What problems need solving
- What sovereign data the UK holds
- What model capability it needs
- What system the government must build around it
- What value the UK can capture
- How the government will measure success
The pilots would also test how different AI systems, including open-weight models and smaller domestic models, can handle different tasks.
The CST called on the government to appoint a single accountable owner for AI sovereignty, such as the head of the Cabinet Office AI Taskforce.
It also wants an AI skills and secondment route to sit alongside the government’s TechFirst programme, plus continued support for low-power computing research.
The council recommended that the government identify important UK datasets and test access arrangements in at least two areas, such as health and creative data.
The CST copied its letter to the Prime Minister, the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the secretaries of state for business, defence and culture.

report.summary: The Alan Turing Institute proposes a free, open, UK-governed AI model built from scratch, backed by government advisers urging sovereign AI capacity and pilots.
report.background: The proposal comes from the Council for Science and Technology, the UK government's top independent science and technology advisory body, in advice published on 19 October and sent to Cabinet Office minister Kanishka Narayan in a letter dated 30 July. It reflects concern that the UK, despite strong research and start-up sectors, relies on foreign-built frontier models and compute. The CST warns that without deliberate action the UK could become a high-value AI customer rather than a country shaping the technology. Its framing of AI sovereignty covers control across compute, data, skills, models, governance and adoption. The Alan Turing Institute's model would be national infrastructure - open, UK-governed and available to researchers, start-ups, small businesses, public services and open-source communities - rather than a proprietary product for one firm or department.
key_points: The Alan Turing Institute wants to build a British AI model from scratch and release it free to the public. The Council for Science and Technology frames it as national infrastructure: an open, UK-governed asset for researchers, start-ups, small businesses, public services and the open-source community, not a proprietary product for a single company or government department.

The CST recommends that government set aside some national AI computing capacity to trial different model types and consider the Turing Institute proposal. These pilots would compare how open-weight models and smaller domestic models handle different tasks, rather than assuming one large foreign model fits every use case.

The council warns the UK risks becoming a 'high-value AI customer' rather than a country that shapes AI and its use. It says the UK should keep access to leading global models but not depend on them for every need, because a specialised UK-built system could perform better in some cases.

The advice includes four recommendations: a UK AI Sovereignty Plan built on an ecosystem map covering compute, data, skills, models, governance and adoption; a single accountable owner for AI sovereignty, suggested as the head of the Cabinet Office AI Taskforce; an AI skills and secondment route alongside TechFirst; and continued support for low-power computing research.

The CST also urges government to identify important UK datasets and test access arrangements in at least two areas, naming health and creative data. Rapid pilots in national security, health and education would each need to answer six questions covering the problem, sovereign data, required model capability, surrounding system, value capture and success measurement.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the proposal signals that sovereign capability is moving from rhetoric to a concrete public-infrastructure idea, potentially creating a UK-governed alternative to US and Chinese models. Developers and start-ups could gain an open-weight base model, shared compute and clearer data-access routes, especially in health and creative sectors. Public services could trial specialised models with UK governance and transparency. Regular users might see better-fit tools and more public scrutiny, but only if government funds compute, secures data deals and appoints accountable leadership. The main risk is that the UK spreads limited resources too thinly and still depends on foreign frontier systems for the hardest tasks.
report.tools: Watch the Alan Turing Institute's proposal and the CST's published advice; track the UK AI Research Resource and Isambard AI for national compute. For hands-on comparison, try open-weight model families such as Llama, Mistral, OLMo and Bloom via Hugging Face, plus evaluation tools like EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness. Follow UK data-access pilots in health and creative sectors.
